title: Question 9

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: why the core is made of iron,

markscheme_points.text: increase flux linkage (with secondary coil) / to reduce flux loss

hints: Hint 1: Think about where the magnetic field produced by the primary coil goes, and what you want as much of it as possible to do at the secondary coil.
parts.proper_answer: The iron core concentrates the magnetic flux and links it to the secondary coil, increasing flux linkage and reducing flux loss.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What the core is for**
Think of the primary coil as making magnetic flux. For the transformer to work well, almost all of that flux needs to pass through the secondary coil. Air is a poor path for flux, it spreads out and leaks away.

Step 2: **Why iron helps**
Iron is easily magnetised and conducts magnetic flux very well. It provides a low-reluctance loop that guides the flux round from primary to secondary, so flux linkage is maximised and leakage is minimised.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: why an electromotive force (e.m.f.) is not induced at the output when a constant direct voltage is at the input.

markscheme_points.text: e.m.f. (induced only) when flux (in core/coil) is changing
constant / direct voltage gives constant flux / field

hints: Hint 1: Recall the condition for an e.m.f. to appear in the secondary coil in terms of what the magnetic flux must be doing.
Hint 2: Compare what a constant d.c. input produces in the core with what an a.c. input produces.
parts.proper_answer: An e.m.f. is induced only when the flux linking the coil is changing. A constant direct voltage produces a constant current and hence constant flux, so rate of change of flux is zero and no e.m.f. is induced.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Faraday's law in words**
Faraday's law says $$E = -N \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t}$$ An e.m.f. $E$ appears only if the flux linkage $N\Phi$ is changing with time. No change, no e.m.f.

Step 2: **Apply to constant d.c.**
A constant direct voltage drives a constant current in the primary. That makes a constant magnetic field and constant flux $\Phi$ in the core. So $$\frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = 0$$ and therefore the induced e.m.f. in the secondary is zero.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: calculate the number of turns of the secondary coil,
hints: Hint 1: Start from Fig. 9.2 and read off the maximum value of the secondary e.m.f. curve, remembering that transformer ratios compare like with like, peak with peak.
Hint 2: Link the primary and secondary voltages to their numbers of turns to solve for the unknown secondary turns.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the secondary peak**
From Fig. 9.2 the secondary e.m.f. $E$ is sinusoidal with peak about $52\text{ V}$. The primary peak is given as $150\text{ V}$. For an ideal transformer peak values obey the same ratio as r.m.s. values.

Step 2: **Use the turns ratio**
For an ideal transformer $$\frac{N_S}{N_P} = \frac{V_S}{V_P}$$ Rearranged: $$N_S = N_P \times \frac{V_S}{V_P}$$ Put numbers in: $$N_S = 1200 \times \frac{52}{150} = 416\text{ turns}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: state one time when the magnetic flux linking the secondary coil is a maximum.

markscheme_points.text: $0 \text{ ms or } 7.5 \text{ ms or } 15.0 \text{ ms or } 22.5 \text{ ms}$

hints: Hint 1: Remember that induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of flux, so think about when the rate of change is zero on a sine curve.
parts.proper_answer: Flux is maximum when $E = 0$, e.g. $t = 0\text{ ms}$ or $7.5\text{ ms}$ or $15.0\text{ ms}$ or $22.5\text{ ms}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link E to flux slope**
Since $$E = -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$$ the e.m.f. is the negative gradient of the flux-time graph. When $E = 0$, the gradient of flux is zero, which is at a peak or trough of flux.

Step 2: **Read zeros from Fig. 9.2**
$E = 0$ at $t = 0$, $7.5\text{ ms}$, $15.0\text{ ms}$ and $22.5\text{ ms}$. At any one of these times the flux linking the secondary is a maximum (in magnitude).

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: A resistor is connected between the output terminals of the secondary coil. The mean power dissipated in the resistor is $1.2\text{ W}$. It may be assumed that the varying voltage across the resistor is equal to the varying e.m.f. $E$ shown in Fig. 9.2.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the resistor.

markscheme_points.text: or mean power $= V^2 / R$ and $V = 52 / \sqrt{2}$ ($= 36.8$ V)

hints: Hint 1: You know the mean power and the peak voltage from the graph, so think about how mean power for a sine wave relates to peak voltage and resistance.
Hint 2: Convert the 52 V peak to the effective steady voltage for heating, or use the peak-power formula with the factor of 2, then rearrange for $R$.
parts.proper_answer: Mean power $= V_0^2/(2R)$ with $V_0 = 52\text{ V}$, so $R = 52^2/(2 \times 1.2) \approx 1.1 \times 10^3\, \Omega$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Mean power with a.c.**
For a resistor the instantaneous power is $V^2/R$. For a sinusoid the mean of $V^2$ over a cycle is $V_0^2/2$, where $V_0$ is the peak. So $$P_{mean} = \frac{V_0^2}{2R}$$ Equivalently, using r.m.s. voltage $V_{rms} = V_0/\sqrt{2}$, $$P_{mean} = \frac{V_{rms}^2}{R}$$

Step 2: **Insert numbers**
Here $V_0 = 52\text{ V}$ and $P_{mean} = 1.2\text{ W}$: $$R = \frac{V_0^2}{2P_{mean}} = \frac{52^2}{2 \times 1.2} = \frac{2704}{2.4} \approx 1130\, \Omega$$ About $1.1 \times 10^3\, \Omega$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (c)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: sinusoidal shape with troughs at zero power
each 'cycle' is 2.4 W high and zero power at correct times

hints: Hint 1: Think about the sign of power when the voltage goes negative, using $P = V^2/R$, and what that means for the shape relative to the time axis.
Hint 2: Compare how often $V$ crosses zero with how often $V^2$ crosses zero to work out how many power pulses fit into 0 to 22.5 ms.
Hint 3: Use the mean power of 1.2 W to work out the height of the power peaks for a sinusoidal-squared variation.
parts.proper_answer: Sketch of $P$ from 0 to 22.5 ms: rectified sinusoidal-squared shape always $\ge 0$ with minima at 0; 3 full power cycles in 22.5 ms; peak $P_0 = 2 \times 1.2 = 2.4\text{ W}$ with zeros at 0, 7.5, 15.0, 22.5 ms.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Shape is always positive**
Power in a resistor is $$P = \frac{V^2}{R}$$ Squaring removes the negative sign, so even when $E$ is negative, $P$ is positive. You get a $\sin^2$ shape that touches zero whenever $V = 0$ and bulges upward in between. It never goes below the time axis.

Step 2: **Frequency is doubled**
$V$ has period $15.0\text{ ms}$ from Fig. 9.2. Since $P$ peaks twice per $V$ cycle (once on positive half, once on negative half), the power period is $$T_P = 15.0/2 = 7.5\text{ ms}$$ From $0$ to $22.5\text{ ms}$ that is $$22.5/7.5 = 3$$ complete power humps, with zeros at $0$, $7.5$, $15.0$ and $22.5\text{ ms}$.

Step 3: **Peak height**
For a $\sin^2$ variation the mean is half the peak. So $$P_{peak} = 2 \times P_{mean} = 2 \times 1.2 = 2.4\text{ W}$$ Draw three identical humps each rising to $2.4\text{ W}$ on the $P/W$ axis up to $3.0\text{ W}$.
